name: byteorder
listed_description: Crate adding extension traits to Read and Write for reading and writing integers and floats with explicit big-endian or little-endian byte order.
reason: No numeric win over a named baseline found. README makes no performance claim and only points to the std to_le_bytes/from_le_bytes methods as an alternative. benches/bench.rs times only byteorder's own BigEndian/LittleEndian/NativeEndian read and write calls, with no hand-written-shift, htonl or ntohl comparison row. Issue #149 compares byteorder write_u64 to hand-written unsafe unaligned pointer writes and the hand-written version is about 2x faster (byteorder loses; no compiler or CPU stated). PR #206 mentions a black_box effect but gives no numbers. Commit 3409ee1 ('perf: convert endianess while reading slice in a single pass') has no benchmark numbers.

name: sha256 (Rust crate)
listed_description: Rust crate used in the book's opening example to hash a file contents with a few lines of code after cargo add sha256.
reason: No benchmark, bench folder or performance claim in the README, source or commit titles; it is a thin wrapper over RustCrypto sha2 with an optional native_openssl feature that calls OpenSSL. Only performance text is issue #9, where a user reports a Node SHA-256 proof-of-work loop much faster than the Rust crate (no numbers) and the maintainer replies that sha2 performance is 'really poor' and suggests the OpenSSL-backed async function. Direction is against the crate, no numbers against OpenSSL SHA256 or Crypto++.
